title: India Opens Insurance to 100% Foreign Ownership — What NRIs Need to Know
excerpt: The landmark reform allows global insurers to fully own Indian companies, promising better products for the diaspora and reshaping a $143 billion market
body:
India has thrown open its insurance sector to full foreign ownership in what may be the most consequential financial sector reform since banking liberalisation in the 1990s. The move, now fully operational after months of legislative and regulatory groundwork, allows global insurers to own 100 percent of Indian insurance companies — a seismic shift from the 74 percent cap that prevailed just months ago.

The reform traces back to December 2025, when Parliament passed the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act. Presidential assent followed on December 20, and most provisions took effect on February 5, 2026. The final piece fell into place on May 2, when the Reserve Bank of India amended the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules to align foreign exchange regulations with the new ownership limits. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade formalised the change through Press Note No. 1 (2026 Series), incorporating it into India's Consolidated FDI Policy.

## What Changed and Why It Matters

Under the old regime, foreign insurers operated through joint ventures with Indian partners, typically holding minority stakes. Even after the 2021 increase to 74 percent, operational constraints — including requirements for majority-Indian boards — kept foreign players from fully committing capital and technology to the Indian market.

The new framework strips away most of those barriers. Foreign insurers can now hold 100 percent of an Indian insurance company under the automatic route, meaning no prior government approval is needed beyond the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India's standard clearance. The only governance requirement: at least one of the chairperson, managing director, or chief executive officer must be a resident Indian citizen.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India retains a special 20 percent FDI cap, preserving the state-owned behemoth's domestic character.

India's insurance penetration stands at just 3.8 percent of GDP — far below the global average of roughly 7 percent. Total premiums reached ₹11.93 lakh crore (approximately $143 billion) in FY2024-25, yet vast swathes of the population remain uninsured, particularly in health and life coverage. IRDAI projects India will become the sixth-largest insurance market globally within the next decade.

## The Global Players Already Moving

The reform has already triggered strategic repositioning. Germany's Allianz exited its 25-year partnership with the Bajaj Group in 2025, selling its 23 percent stake in Bajaj General Insurance and Bajaj Life Insurance. Within months, Allianz entered a 50:50 binding agreement with Mukesh Ambani-backed Jio Financial Services for reinsurance, general insurance, and life insurance joint ventures — clearly anticipating the higher ownership ceiling.

Other global giants — AXA, Zurich, and Prudential among them — are expected to reassess their India strategies. The 100 percent cap means a foreign insurer can now build and brand a fully owned Indian subsidiary, deploying its global technology stack, actuarial models, and digital distribution platforms without negotiating control with a local partner.

## What This Means for the NRI Community

For the estimated 32 million Indians living abroad, the reform opens several practical possibilities. Global insurers entering India with full ownership are likely to offer cross-border products tailored to diaspora needs: health insurance that covers treatment in both India and the country of residence, life policies with seamless NRI premium payment, and pension products designed for eventual return migration.

Currently, NRIs navigating Indian insurance face a patchwork of restrictions — limited online access, rupee-only premium payment, and policy servicing that assumes a resident Indian. A fully foreign-owned insurer with a global operations backbone could solve many of these friction points.

The reform also carries investment implications. NRIs holding Indian equities should watch listed insurers closely. New entrants backed by deep global capital could compress margins for smaller domestic players, while well-positioned incumbents with distribution networks — think HDFC Life, SBI Life, and ICICI Prudential — may become acquisition targets or find partnership valuations rising.

## Risks and Open Questions

Not everything is settled. The composite licence framework promised alongside the FDI reform — which would allow a single entity to underwrite both life and general insurance — has not yet been fully operationalised. Smaller domestic insurers worry that deep-pocketed global entrants could trigger a price war, particularly in motor and health segments where margins are already thin.

There are also questions about whether the reform will actually translate into rapid capital inflows. India's regulatory environment, while improving, remains complex. IRDAI approval is still required for every new entrant, and the regulator has signalled it will scrutinise the "fit and proper" credentials of foreign promoters carefully.

## What's Next

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman first signalled the 100 percent FDI move in the Union Budget for 2026, framing it as part of India's broader push to attract long-term institutional capital. For the diaspora, the practical impact may take 18 to 24 months to materialise as global insurers file applications, secure IRDAI approval, and build distribution networks. But the direction is unmistakable: India wants the world's largest insurers fully invested in its market, and it has removed the last ownership barrier to make that happen.
